section_summary: This section concludes a British commercial report on Formosa and contains Oswald White’s detailed report on trade and economic conditions in colonial Korea, including extensive appendices on Japan’s imports and exports. It then shifts to State Department file notes, a 1930 report on Japan’s depression, and correspondence concerning Robert Preston Brooks’s observations on China and Japan. The final pages comprise a 1932 series of Embassy telegrams surveying Japanese finance, the budget, cotton, silk, metals, cement, shipping, shipbuilding, and electric power.

subfiles.title: Report on the Trade of Formosa for 1929 and Conditions to 1930, conclusion
subfiles.about: Concludes an assessment of Formosa’s imports, foreign trade, shipping, ports, roads, and railways.
subfiles.summary: The report discusses opium, cotton textiles, and Formosa’s trade with the British Empire, China, and the United States. It notes that customs statistics understate foreign goods transshipped through Japan. The concluding pages describe shipping services, harbor expansion at Keelung and Takao, and road and railway construction across the island.

subfiles.title: Report on the Trade of Corea for 1929 and Conditions to June 1930
subfiles.from: Oswald White, His Majesty’s Consul-General at Seoul
subfiles.about: Surveys Korean economic conditions and trade and supplies statistical appendices on Japan’s foreign commerce.
subfiles.summary: White describes Korea’s depressed economy, poor rice harvests, restricted credit, and dependence on Japanese finance and markets. Detailed sections cover rice, fertilizers, flour, textiles, machinery, motor vehicles, petroleum, timber, silk, mining, and marine products. Appendices list Japan’s principal imports, exports, sources, and destinations for 1929, with special attention to British trade. The report ends with a catalogue of Department of Overseas Trade publications and a printer’s colophon.

subfiles.title: Index Bureau cross-reference for Forbes’s October 6 economic report
subfiles.to: Department of State decimal file 894.00 P R/34
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to Forbes’s report on Japan’s economic situation and industrial production curtailment.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references file 894.50/53 to another Department of State filing. It identifies a report from Forbes dated October 6, 1930, concerning the economic situation and production cuts in selected industries.

subfiles.title: Embassy monthly report extract on Japan’s economic situation
subfiles.about: Reviews unsuccessful economic-relief discussions, industrial production cuts, and tentative signs of recovery in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The extract says official and industrial discussions of rationalization, coordinated credit, and rural relief had produced no concrete results by the end of September. It lists severe production curtailments in cotton spinning, silk, rayon, hemp, chemicals, paper, lime, cement, and iron and steel. Rising coal activity and cotton-cloth exports suggested a possible recovery, though informed observers remained cautious.

subfiles.title: Index Bureau cross-reference for Johnson’s conversation with Veach and Brooks
subfiles.about: Cross-references Johnson’s account of a conversation about economic conditions in China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet identifies a Johnson document dated October 25, 1930. It describes the subject as a conversation with Reverend Robert Wells Veach and Professor Robert Preston Brooks concerning China and Japan.

subfiles.title: Despatch 546 transmitting a memorandum of conversation with Veach and Brooks
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Minister, Peiping
subfiles.about: Transmits a memorandum recording Brooks’s and Veach’s observations on economic conditions in China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson forwards a memorandum of his October 2 conversation with Reverend Robert Wells Veach and Professor Robert Preston Brooks. Brooks, traveling under a Kahn fellowship, offered no constructive conclusions about China but anticipated difficulties in overpopulated and overindustrialized Japan. A copy was sent to the American Embassy in Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on conditions in China and Japan
subfiles.about: Records Robert Preston Brooks’s pessimistic assessment of China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Brooks said China’s underlying conditions were too difficult to determine reliably and that his monograph might have to leave the country largely untreated. He argued that Japan was overpopulated and overindustrialized and faced pressure from diminishing food returns. He also believed Japan’s industrial expansion depended excessively on a turbulent and hostile Chinese market.

subfiles.title: Department telegram 75 requesting a comprehensive Japanese economic and financial report
subfiles.from: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson
subfiles.about: Orders a detailed report on Japan’s finances, currency, budget, banking, cotton manufacturing, and shipping.
subfiles.summary: The Department requests the fullest report possible on Japanese government and bank balances abroad, foreign debt, invisible balance-of-payments items, currency, prices, living costs, and the budget. It also asks for the condition of cotton manufacturing, shipping, and banking. Important findings were to be telegraphed, with the complete report sent by mail, and Consul Dickover was suggested as an assistant.

subfiles.title: Follow-up telegram recommending Garrels and Dickover
subfiles.from: Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson
subfiles.about: Suggests using Garrels as well as Dickover to help prepare the requested economic report.
subfiles.summary: Stimson follows up the Department’s earlier instruction for a Japanese economic and financial survey. He recommends that the Embassy enlist both Garrels and Dickover in the work.

subfiles.title: Telegram 105 outlining the Embassy’s reporting plan
subfiles.from: W. Cameron Forbes, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Explains that the Embassy will send a sectional telegraphic summary followed by a complete mailed report.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy agrees to report separately on the different phases of Japanese finance, commerce, and industry and then provide a general summary. The sectional telegrams will all use the number 107 and will be followed by a complete report by mail.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section A—Finance
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports difficulty obtaining authoritative information on Japan’s foreign balances and indebtedness.
subfiles.summary: The Commercial Attaché could not secure exact figures for stock balances, bills, and other outstanding obligations abroad. The Finance Department said that Diet business left it unable to answer individual inquiries at that time.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section B—Cotton
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Assesses production, stocks, exports, and the financial condition of Japan’s cotton industry.
subfiles.summary: Cotton was considered healthier than most Japanese industries, with 1931 increases in raw-cotton imports and consumption and in yarn production, although textile exports declined. Large inventories bought cheaply before the gold embargo strengthened major firms, while smaller concerns faced greater difficulty. Exports were falling because of adverse conditions in China and British India, threatening future performance.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section C—Expense of Budget
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese supplementary borrowing and expenditures associated with the Manchurian Incident.
subfiles.summary: The Diet authorized a 67.5-million-yen loan in addition to emergency loans previously approved by the Privy Council. The Finance Minister requested further funds for expenses arising from the Manchurian Incident, bringing the additional expenditure described to 137.41 million yen. The government could draw partly upon special-account balances and the postal deposit bureau, while payments into the sinking fund were reduced.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section D—Silk
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Estimates the Japanese silk industry’s debts, bank exposure, inventories, and losses.
subfiles.summary: Because silk production was dispersed among farmers and filatures, invested capital could not be measured accurately. The Commercial Attaché estimated more than 250 million yen in outstanding obligations, including loans secured by over 100,000 bales of old silk. With prices near 650 yen per bale and profitability requiring roughly 800 yen, many reelers could not pay interest and banks faced potentially heavy liquidation losses.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section E—Iron and Steel
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Summarizes capital, debts, losses, and structural disadvantages in Japan’s iron and steel industry.
subfiles.summary: Paid-up capital was estimated at 385 million yen, including about 140 million yen of government investment in the Yawata Steel Works, while private-company obligations approached 320 million yen. The industry was operating at a loss and remained handicapped by dependence on imported ore and other raw materials.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section F—Copper
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese copper output, trade, capitalization, profitability, and domestic demand.
subfiles.summary: Japan produced 74,800 metric tons of copper in 1931 and exported 26,600 tons, largely as bars sent to Russia. Although copper prices were unsatisfactory, the four principal producers were considered financially sound because gold and silver by-products supported profitability. Electrification provided a steady domestic market.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section G—Cement
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Provides production, trade, and capitalization figures for Japan’s cement industry.
subfiles.summary: The Commercial Attaché estimated cement-industry capital at about 200 million yen. Annual output had been roughly 3.7 million tons, with exports of 450,000 tons and imports of 10,000 tons. Conditions were unsatisfactory, but the industry was believed to remain fundamentally sound.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section H—Shipping
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes Japanese shipping-company finances, fleet size, laid-up tonnage, and declining foreign earnings.
subfiles.summary: Department of Communications figures listed 841 shipping companies with 493 million yen in capital and a collective net loss exceeding 13 million yen. Japan’s register contained 914 vessels over 1,000 tons, while 356 vessels totaling 350,000 tons were laid up. Foreign earnings were expected to fall sharply because sterling had depreciated and China-bound cargo had declined.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section I—Shipbuilding
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports losses, weak orders, and a poor outlook in Japanese shipbuilding.
subfiles.summary: Seventy-seven shipbuilding companies held 238 million yen in paid-up capital and 36 million yen in reserves, while reporting losses exceeding five million yen. Preliminary evidence showed most yards operating unprofitably, with little new construction planned and poor prospects for the coming year.

subfiles.title: Telegram 107, Section J—Electric Light and Power
subfiles.from: Edwin L. Neville, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Examines capitalization and foreign-loan exposure in Japan’s electric light and power industry.
subfiles.summary: The Commercial Attaché placed total industry capital at three billion yen, of which about 1.3 billion represented strictly electric light and power concerns. Five named Japanese companies carried substantial foreign loans whose yen burden had risen after exchange depreciation; the Taiwan Power Company also had major foreign obligations. The companies were expected to meet their debts by reducing dividends, although lower rates and higher fuel costs had weakened income.
